text:
Natasha did not remember how that day passed, or the night, or the next day and the next night. She did not sleep and did not leave her mother’s side. Natasha’s love, steadfast and patient, not as an explanation, not as consolation, but as a summons to life, seemed every second to embrace the countess from all sides. On the third night the countess grew quiet for several minutes, and Natasha closed her eyes, resting her head on the arm of the chair. The bed creaked; Natasha opened her eyes. The countess was sitting up in bed and speaking softly.

“How glad I am that you have come. You are tired; would you like some tea?” Natasha went over to her. “You have grown more handsome and manly,” the countess continued, taking her daughter by the hand.

“Mamma, what are you saying!…”

“Natasha, he is gone, gone forever!” And, embracing her daughter, the countess began to weep for the first time.

III.

Princess Marya postponed her departure. Sonya and the count tried to take Natasha’s place, but they could not. They saw that she alone could keep her mother from mad despair. For three weeks Natasha remained constantly at her mother’s side, slept in an armchair in her room, gave her drink and food, and talked to her without ceasing—talked because her tender, caressing voice alone soothed the countess.

The mother’s spiritual wound could not heal. Petya’s death had torn away half her life. A month after the news of Petya’s death, which had found her a fresh and vigorous woman of fifty, she emerged from her room half dead and taking no part in life—an old woman. But the same wound that had half killed the countess, this new wound, called Natasha back to life.

A spiritual wound caused by the rending of a spiritual being, strange though it may seem, closes little by little, just like a physical wound. And after a deep wound has healed and its edges seem to have come together, a spiritual wound, like a physical one, heals only through the force of life pushing outward from within.

Natasha’s wound healed in the same way. She thought that her life was over. But suddenly her love for her mother showed her that the essence of her life—love—was still alive within her. Love awoke, and life awoke.

Prince Andrei’s last days had bound Natasha to Princess Marya. The new misfortune brought them still closer together. Princess Marya postponed her departure and, for the last three weeks, tended Natasha as though she were a sick child. The final weeks Natasha had spent in her mother’s room had undermined her physical strength.

One day in the middle of the day, Princess Marya, noticing that Natasha was trembling with a feverish chill, took her to her own room and put her to bed. Natasha lay down, but when Princess Marya, after lowering the blinds, was about to leave, Natasha called her over.

“I do not want to sleep. Marie, sit with me.”

“You are tired—try to fall asleep.”

“No, no. Why did you take me away? She will ask for me.”

“She is much better. She spoke so well today,” said Princess Marya.

Natasha lay in bed and, in the room’s half-darkness, studied Princess Marya’s face.

“Does she look like him?” Natasha thought. “Yes, she does and she does not. But she is special, a stranger, entirely new, unknown. And she loves me. What is in her soul? Everything good. But how? How does she think? How does she look at me? Yes, she is beautiful.”

“Masha,” she said, timidly drawing her hand toward her. “Masha, do not think that I am bad. No? Masha, darling. How I love you. Let us be completely, completely friends.”

And Natasha, embracing her, began kissing Princess Marya’s hands and face. Princess Marya was embarrassed and delighted by this expression of Natasha’s feelings.

From that day onward, there arose between Princess Marya and Natasha that passionate and tender friendship which exists only between women. They kissed constantly, said tender words to each other, and spent most of their time together. If one went out, the other became anxious and hurried to join her. Together they felt greater harmony with each other than they did apart, each alone with herself. A feeling stronger than friendship arose between them: it was the exclusive feeling that life was possible only in each other’s presence.

Sometimes they were silent for hours at a time; sometimes, already lying in their beds, they began to talk and talked until morning. They spoke mostly of the distant past. Princess Marya told of her childhood, of her mother, of her father, of her dreams; and Natasha, who before had turned away with calm incomprehension from this life of devotion and submission, from the poetry of Christian self-renunciation, now, feeling herself bound to Princess Marya by love, came to love Princess Marya’s past as well and understood the aspect of life that had previously been incomprehensible to her. She did not think of applying submission and self-renunciation to her own life, because she was accustomed to seeking other joys, but she understood and came to love in another this virtue that had previously been incomprehensible to her. For Princess Marya, who listened to stories of Natasha’s childhood and early youth, a previously incomprehensible aspect of life was likewise revealed: faith in life, in the pleasures of life.

Still, just as before, they did not speak of him, so as not to disturb with words what seemed to them the loftiness of the feeling within them; and this silence about him caused them, little by little and without believing it, to forget him.

Natasha grew thin and pale and became so physically weak that everyone constantly spoke about her health, and this pleased her. But sometimes she was unexpectedly seized not only by fear of death, but by fear of illness, weakness, and loss of beauty; and at times she involuntarily examined her bare arm attentively, amazed at its thinness, or in the mornings stared in the mirror at her elongated, pitiful face, as it seemed to her. It seemed to her that this was how it had to be, and at the same time she grew frightened and sad.

Once she went upstairs quickly and became heavily out of breath. At once, involuntarily, she invented an errand for herself downstairs, and from there ran upstairs again, testing her strength and observing herself.

Another time she called Dunyasha, and her voice quavered. She called her once more, even though she could hear her footsteps—called in that full, deep voice in which she used to sing, and listened to it.

She did not know it and would not have believed it, but beneath the layer of silt that seemed to her impenetrable and had covered her soul, slender, tender young blades of grass were already pushing through; they were destined to take root and so cover with their living shoots the grief that had crushed her that it would soon be neither visible nor noticeable. The wound was healing from within.

At the end of January Princess Marya left for Moscow, and the count insisted that Natasha go with her in order to consult the doctors.
